title: Federal Judge Temporarily Blocks Border Wall Work in Texas' Big Bend
summary:
A federal court in Texas on Friday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and other infrastructure across the state's Big Bend region. The ruling pauses construction while the court considers a legal challenge; it does not settle the case.

The order includes Big Bend National Park, which sits on a bend of the Rio Grande River. It also covers the entire Big Bend border sector, roughly 500 miles long. That is about a quarter of the roughly 2,000-mile southern border with Mexico.

The projects are part of a $46 billion administration effort that includes 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology. Landowners, businesses and environmentalists in the region have united in opposition.

Opponents argue that the area's remote location and rugged landscape already discourage illegal border crossings. They also say the administration violated the law by issuing waivers to bypass regulations. A waiver allows an exception to a rule. The lawsuit challenges bypassing rules intended to protect the environment, culture and archaeology. It was brought by an environmental organization, advocates for a historic church in Ruidosa and a river guide.

Judge Kathleen Cardone said the plaintiffs, the people bringing the lawsuit, were likely to succeed on at least one claim. She also found that they were likely to suffer serious harm that could not be undone without an injunction, a court order that stops an action. She said the public interest favored granting the order. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The first wall panels went up in the sector in mid-September. Bulldozers clearing land in the national park in August prompted opposition from both Republicans and Democrats. Customs and Border Protection paused activity there, but that pause expired on September 30. The administration says it is reevaluating plans for the park and has not announced its decision.

Park advocates welcomed the ruling. Tiernan Sittenfeld, president and CEO of the National Parks Conservation Association, called for the administration to repair damage, meet with border communities and find other solutions.
why_it_matters: The case concerns how government construction plans interact with environmental and cultural protection rules. The temporary order affects Big Bend National Park and the wider border sector.
